item.content:encoded:
Build Your Own Agent Ecosystem: Lessons from Developing QuantVault

I built QuantVault, a multi-agent runtime that deploys specialist AI personas from a single FastAPI backend. The system uses LangGraph to orchestrate the agents and allows for easy swapping of personalities and tools via YAML profiles. A React dashboard provides an intuitive interface for routing tasks, uploading knowledge, and monitoring execution.

The QuantVault system has three profiles, each with a unique role and set of tools. The first profile, “market_analyst,” is a quantitative financial volatility research analyst that uses tools such as “aws_bridge.read_s3_data_lake,” “data_sandbox.execute_secure_python,” and “query_company_knowledge” to read historical pricing data, measure volatility, and output structured markdown execution reports.

The second profile, “ai_trust,” is an enterprise AI trust and data governance lead that ensures all data passing through the system is sanitized, secure, and compliant. This profile uses tools such as “pii_regex_masker” and “query_company_knowledge” to identify and mask personally identifiable information (PII) such as phone numbers, emails, or social security numbers.

The third profile, “outbound_sdr,” is a senior SaaS outbound sales development representative that drafts hyper-personalized, concise, and high-converting cold emails based on prospect data. This profile uses tools such as “crm_data_fetcher” and “query_company_knowledge” to fetch prospect data and draft emails that get straight to the value proposition.

The supervisor is a key component of the QuantVault system, automatically delegating user prompts to the best specialist agent based on the prompt. The system also has a built-in tool ecosystem that provides functionality such as PII masking, CRM lookup, and RAG search, as well as LLM fallbacks that provide redundancy and fault tolerance.

One of the key benefits of the QuantVault system is its flexibility and scalability. The use of YAML profiles allows for easy swapping of personalities and tools without changing the core code, making it simple to deploy specialist AI personas and adapt to changing requirements. The system also provides a high level of security and compliance, with features such as secure Python validation scripts and PII masking.

The QuantVault system is now built and working, providing a powerful solution for deploying specialist AI personas. The system has a wide range of potential applications, from financial analysis and data governance to sales and marketing. By using the QuantVault system, organizations can simplify the deployment of specialist AI personas and make it more efficient, allowing them to focus on high-value tasks and drive business success.

One specific thing that other developers can apply to their own work is the use of YAML profile-based approach for defining agents. This approach allows for easy swapping of personalities and tools without changing the core code and provides a flexible and scalable solution for deploying specialist AI personas. By using this approach, developers can simplify the deployment of specialist AI personas and make it more efficient, allowing them to focus on high-value tasks and drive business success.

The implementation of the QuantVault system involved several key components, including the AgentChassis, YAML profiles, tool ecosystem, and LLM fallbacks. The AgentChassis is a LangGraph agent orchestra that manages the lifecycle of the agents, while the YAML profiles define the personalities and tools for each agent. The tool ecosystem provides a set of built-in tools that provide functionality such as PII masking, CRM lookup, and RAG search, while the LLM fallbacks provide redundancy and fault tolerance.

The QuantVault system also has a set of API routes that provide access to the system’s functionality. The /health API route returns the health status of the system, while the /upload API route uploads a file to the local Chroma vector store. The /supervisor API route automatically delegates user prompts to the best specialist agent, while the /run/{profile} API route runs an agent with the specified profile.

Overall, the QuantVault system is a powerful solution for deploying specialist AI personas. Its flexibility, scalability, and security make it an ideal choice for organizations looking to simplify the deployment of specialist AI personas and drive business success. By using the QuantVault system, developers can focus on high-value tasks and drive business success, while also providing a high level of security and compliance.

item.title: The 2-Hour Gigabyte: Why Nigeria’s Internet is a Trap
item.dc:creator: Agoro Oluwatimilehin
item.content:encoded:
We aren’t just paying for data. We are paying for transparency failures, diesel ghost-costs, and 3G speeds at 5G prices.

I’ve always been curious why the internet in Nigeria feels like a leaky pocket. You know the vibe: You buy 20GB, you blink, and you get that “You have used 75% of your data bundle” text.

For years, I assumed I was just scrolling too much Instagram. Then I stopped guessing and started coding.

I built a custom scraper to analyze pricing data from 2021 to 2025 for MTN, Airtel, and Glo. I also dug into the audited Sustainability Reports of the infrastructure giants that actually own the towers (IHS and ATC), and cross-referenced it all with Ookla Speedtest Intelligence reports.

What I found isn’t just “inflation.” It is a system of incentives that rewards inefficiency while bleeding your wallet dry.

Here is the data-driven truth about why you are broke.

1. The “Time Bandit” (It’s Not Price, It’s Validity)

If you look at the headline numbers, telcos will argue that data is “cheaper” today. In 2021, ₦1,000 got you roughly 1.5GB. Today, ₦1,000 still gets you roughly 1.5GB.

But that’s a lie by omission. The price didn’t change the calendar did.

Here is the breakdown from my dataset:

  • 2021 (MTN/Airtel): ₦1,000 Plan = 1.5GB for 30 Days
  • 2025 (MTN/Airtel): ₦1,000 Plan = 1.5GB for 7 Days

This is Shrinkflation.

By quietly killing the monthly validity on entry-level plans, the system forces users to renew four times a month. To stay online for 30 days now, you don’t pay ₦1,000; you pay ₦4,000.

The Outlier: My data shows Glo is the last line of defense, maintaining the 30-day validity at the ₦1,000 price point. If they shift, the entry barrier for the Nigerian internet doubles overnight.

2. The Poverty Premium (The Math)

I wanted to know if this was just a “Global Economy” problem. So, I ran a benchmark: “How long does a minimum wage earner have to work to buy 1GB of data?”

To ensure we are fair, here is the math:

  • Nigeria Min Wage: ₦70,000/month. Assuming a standard 160-hour work month, that is ₦437.50/hour.
  • Average Data Cost: ~₦1,000 for a standard monthly 1GB bundle.

The Result:

  • 🇺🇸 USA ($7.25/hr): It takes 41 minutes of work to buy 1GB.
  • 🇳🇬 Nigeria (₦437/hr): It takes 2 Hours and 17 Minutes of work.

Think about that. An American works less than an hour for their data. You work until lunch break just to afford the connection to do the work.

We aren’t paying a utility bill; we are paying a “Poverty Tax” on access.

3. The Quality Gap: Paying More for Less

It gets worse. Not only do we work 3x longer to afford data, but the product we buy is objectively inferior.

I pulled the median download speed data from Ookla Speedtest Intelligence (Q1 2024) to compare what “1GB” actually feels like in these countries.

  • USA: 113.13 Mbps (Blazing fast 5G standard).
  • South Africa: 63.45 Mbps (Solid 4G+/5G).
  • Nigeria: 26.48 Mbps (Struggling 4G).

The Trap: We are paying a premium price (in terms of labor hours) for a product that is 4x slower than the US standard and half the speed of South Africa. We are buying a Ferrari engine but getting a Corolla.

4. The Solar Disconnect

This is where the public narrative falls apart.

Every time consumers complain about cost, the industry points to diesel prices: “Diesel is ₦1,400 per liter! We are bleeding!”

While diesel costs have risen, the corporate reality is different. I analyzed the 2023 Sustainability Reports for the tower companies — documents filed with investors where they are legally required to be accurate.

  • The Narrative: “Rising diesel consumption is unsustainable.”
  • The Data: In 2023 alone, IHS Towers reported reducing their diesel consumption by 30.2 Million Liters (Source: IHS 2023 Report, p. 31). ATC Nigeria cut theirs by 43.5 Million Liters (Source: ATC Sustainability Report).

They have successfully switched thousands of towers to Solar Hybrid systems, saving billions of Naira in fuel costs.

This is good business. But here is the issue: The price you pay for data is still calculated as if they are burning diesel 24/7.

The savings from this massive solar transition aren’t being passed down to the consumer; they are being absorbed into the margin. The system incentivizes them to keep the “Diesel Crisis” narrative alive because it justifies high prices, even as they silently disconnect the generators.

The Verdict

The problem isn’t just that we are poor. The problem is that the market structure allows operators to double-dip: charging us for the inefficiency of the grid while pocketing the savings from their own solar solutions.

Nigeria doesn’t have an internet problem. It has a transparency problem and the poor are paying interest on it.

Sources & Notes

  • Data Collection: Pricing data scraped via Python from USSD archives (*141#, *312#) and web.archive.org (2021–2025).
  • Minimum Wage: Based on the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Act 2024 (₦70,000).
  • Internet Speed: Ookla Speedtest Global Index (Q1 2024).
  • Solar Data: Extracted from IHS Towers 2023 Sustainability Report and ATC Africa Sustainability Overview.
